questions.question: You run `node greet.ts` using Node's built-in type stripping, and the file contains a type error (a number passed where a string is expected). What happens?
options: Node refuses to start and prints the TypeScript error
Node prints a warning with the error code, then runs the file
Node deletes the type annotations and runs the code without reporting the type error
Node compiles the file with tsc first, so the error is reported
questions.explanation: Type stripping only removes the annotations; Node never type-checks. The call simply runs as JavaScript. That is why `tsc --noEmit` (or the editor) is still needed to catch type errors. Node does not invoke tsc or print type diagnostics.

questions.question: Which `tsc` flag type-checks the project but writes no output files (the usual choice in CI)?
questions.explanation: `tsc --noEmit` runs the full type check and emits nothing. By default `tsc` writes JavaScript even when there are errors, so CI usually runs `tsc --noEmit` and fails the build on any error.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for `gst`?
questions.code: const gst = 0.18;
questions.explanation: A `const` can never be reassigned, so TypeScript keeps the exact literal type `0.18`. With `let gst = 0.18` the type would widen to `number`, because a `let` may later hold another number.

questions.question: Compiling this with `--strict` reports one error. What is its error code?
questions.code:
let v: unknown = "hi";
v.toUpperCase();
questions.explanation: `unknown` accepts any value but cannot be used until you narrow it, so calling a method on it fails with TS18046: "'v' is of type 'unknown'". With `any` instead of `unknown`, the line would compile and could crash at runtime.

questions.question: Given these overloads, what happens on the last line?
options: `r` is typed `number | number[]`, matching the implementation signature
`r` is typed `number`, because the first overload is chosen
Compile error: no overload matches this call
questions.explanation: Callers only see the overload signatures, never the implementation signature. A `string | string[]` argument fits neither `(value: string)` nor `(value: string[])` on its own, so the compiler reports TS2769 "No overload matches this call". The implementation's `string | string[]` parameter is not callable from outside.

questions.question: Which line(s) cause a compile error?
questions.explanation: Excess property checking applies only to fresh object literals, so line A fails: 'coupon' does not exist in type 'Order'. Line B assigns a variable; ordinary assignability is structural and only needs `id` and `amount`, so the extra property is allowed.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for `pair`?
questions.code: const pair = ["Rent", 25000];
questions.answerHint: Type the type exactly as TypeScript would show it
questions.explanation: An array literal without an annotation is inferred as an array, not a tuple, so the element type is the union `string | number`. To get a tuple, annotate it (`[string, number]`) or use `as const`.

questions.question: Which of these can be written with a `type` alias but NOT with an `interface`?
options: An object with an index signature
questions.explanation: An interface can only describe an object shape. A type alias can name any type, including unions, tuples and primitives. Optional properties, methods and index signatures work in both.

questions.question: What is the type of `ChildT["id"]`?
questions.code:
interface Base { id: string }
type ChildT = Base & { id: number };
questions.explanation: An intersection requires both shapes at once, so `id` becomes `string & number`, which is impossible and reduces to `never`. Unlike `interface Child extends Base { id: number }`, which errors immediately, `&` silently produces the impossible type. It is not `string | number`; that would be a union.

questions.question: Which call is a compile error?
questions.explanation: `const s1 = "paid"` keeps the literal type `"paid"`, which fits `PaymentStatus`. `let s2 = "paid"` is widened to `string` because it could be reassigned, and a general `string` is not assignable to the literal union.

questions.question: Inside the `if` block, what is the type of `input`?
questions.explanation: `typeof null === "object"`, so a `typeof` check alone does not remove `null`; the narrowed type still includes it, and calling `Object.keys(input)` would fail. You also need `input !== null` (or a truthiness check). `object | string[]` is the tempting answer, but it forgets that classic trap.

questions.question: The `rectangle` case was forgotten. What error code does the compiler report on the `const unhandled: never = s;` line?
questions.explanation: After the handled cases are narrowed away, `s` is still the rectangle member. Assigning it to `never` fails with TS2322 ("Type '{ kind: "rectangle"; ... }' is not assignable to type 'never'"). That is the exhaustiveness check: add the missing case and the error disappears.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered }
console.log(OrderStatus[1]);
questions.explanation: Numeric enums are numbered from 0 and compile to a real object that maps both ways, so `OrderStatus[1]` is the reverse lookup `"Shipped"`. `OrderStatus.Shipped` would print 1. String enums have no reverse mapping.

questions.question: What is the type of `cap`?
questions.explanation: `as const` infers the narrowest literal types and makes everything readonly, and `satisfies` checks the shape without widening it. So `FEES.CARD.capRupees` keeps the literal type `2500`. With a plain `Record<string, FeeRule>` annotation it would be `number`.

questions.question: With the annotation below, what is `keyof typeof FEES`?
questions.explanation: An annotation makes the variable become the annotated type, so `typeof FEES` is just `Record<string, FeeRule>` and its keys are `string`. The specific keys are lost. Using `satisfies Record<string, FeeRule>` instead keeps the inferred type, and then `keyof typeof FEES` would be `"UPI" | "CARD"`.

questions.question: What does the last line print?
questions.explanation: TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time check only; the emitted JavaScript has a normal `secret` property, so `JSON.stringify` includes it. `#hidden` is a real JavaScript private field and is invisible to `JSON.stringify`, `Object.keys` and bracket access.

questions.question: Which statement is true of an abstract class but NOT of an interface?
options: It exists at runtime and works with `instanceof`
A class can implement several of them at once
questions.explanation: An abstract class is a real JavaScript class, so it exists at runtime, can hold shared implementation, and works with `instanceof`. Interfaces are erased. A class can `implements` several interfaces but can `extends` only one class, so the second option describes interfaces, not abstract classes.

questions.question: What is the type of `a`?
questions.explanation: `T` is inferred from the argument as `number`, and the declared return type is `T | undefined`, so `a` is `number | undefined`. Inference keeps the element type, which is the point of using a type parameter instead of `any`.

questions.question: What is the type of `x`?
questions.answerHint: Type the type exactly as TypeScript would show it
questions.explanation: Nothing at the call site mentions `T`, so inference has nothing to work with and falls back to `unknown`, giving `unknown[]`. Pass the type explicitly, as in `emptyList<string>()`, to get `string[]`.

questions.question: What is the type of `amt`?
questions.explanation: `K` is inferred as the literal `"amountRupees"`, and the return type `T[K]` looks up that property's type, `number`. If the signature used `key: keyof T` with return type `T[keyof T]`, every call would return `string | number`; the separate `K` remembers which key was passed.

questions.question: Why does the `return` line fail to compile?
options: `{ length: 0 }` does not satisfy the constraint `{ length: number }`
Generic functions cannot return object literals
The constraint should use `implements` instead of `extends`
The caller chooses `T`; it could be a different subtype such as `string`, and `{ length: 0 }` is not that type
questions.explanation: Satisfying the constraint is not the same as being `T`. If someone calls `emptyOf("abc")`, `T` is `string`, and `{ length: 0 }` is not a string, hence TS2322 "'T' could be instantiated with a different subtype of constraint". The object literal does satisfy the constraint, so the first option is wrong.

questions.question: Which utility type filters the members of a union type (rather than the keys of an object type)?
questions.explanation: `Exclude<U, X>` removes union members assignable to `X` (and `Extract` keeps them). `Pick` and `Omit` work on the keys of an object type, and `Partial` changes property modifiers.

questions.question: Does the last line compile, and why?
options: No: `vpa` is required for the upi variant
Yes: `Omit` on a union keeps only the keys shared by all members, so `vpa` is lost
No: `Omit` cannot be applied to a union
Yes: `Omit` makes all remaining properties optional
questions.explanation: `Omit` does not distribute over a union. It works on the keys common to every member (`kind` and `id`), so the result is `{ kind: "upi" | "card" }` and variant-specific fields like `vpa` disappear. `Omit` does not make properties optional; it simply dropped them. The fix is a distributive helper built with a conditional type.

questions.question: A project compiles with `tsc` using `"module": "nodenext"` and runs the emitted `.js`. How should `checkout.ts` import from `money.ts` in the same folder?
options: `import { withGst } from "./money.ts";` with no extra options
questions.explanation: Under `nodenext`, TypeScript follows Node's ES module rules, which need full file extensions, and you write the extension of the output file that will exist at runtime. TypeScript maps `./money.js` back to `money.ts` while checking. Leaving the extension off gives error TS2835; `./money.ts` needs options such as `allowImportingTsExtensions` or `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`.

questions.question: In a `.d.ts` file, which keyword in front of a function or const means "this exists at runtime; trust me about its type" (it has no implementation)?
questions.explanation: `declare` introduces an ambient declaration: a type for JavaScript that exists elsewhere, with no implementation. Generated declaration files contain lines like `export declare function withGst(amountRupees: number): number;`.

questions.question: A project sets `"target": "es2015"` and uses `Array.prototype.at`. Which statement is correct?
options: `target` adds a polyfill for `at`, so it works on old browsers
`target` and `lib` are two names for the same setting
`target` makes the compiler reject any API newer than ES2015 at runtime
`target` controls the emitted syntax; `lib` controls which built-in APIs are typed, and neither adds polyfills
questions.explanation: `target` decides which JavaScript syntax is emitted (newer syntax is down-levelled); `lib` decides which built-in APIs the checker knows about. TypeScript never polyfills runtime methods such as `Array.prototype.at`, so the first option is a common misconception.

questions.question: Which comment directive suppresses the error on the next line but itself becomes an error once that line no longer has an error?
questions.explanation: `// @ts-expect-error` is preferred over `// @ts-ignore` because it reports an unused directive when the problem is fixed, so stale suppressions do not pile up. `@ts-ignore` silently stays forever.

questions.question: Which type is the usual choice for a component's `children` prop, accepting elements, strings, numbers, `null` and arrays of these?
questions.explanation: `ReactNode` is the widest renderable type and fits `children`. `JSX.Element` and `ReactElement` mean a single JSX element only, so they reject plain strings or `null`. `HTMLElement` is a DOM type, not a React one.

questions.question: Without `as const`, what type does this custom hook return?
questions.explanation: A returned array literal is inferred as an array of the union of its element types, so callers destructuring `[isOpen, toggle]` get `boolean | (() => void)` for both and cannot call `toggle`. Adding `as const` gives the tuple `readonly [boolean, () => void]`.

questions.question: An Express handler is typed `Request<{}, FundResponse, CreateFundBody>`. A client posts `{ "navInr": "lots" }`. What happens?
options: Nothing checks it at runtime: the code receives the bad value even though `req.body` is typed `CreateFundBody`
Express rejects the request with 400 because the body does not match the type
TypeScript throws a runtime TypeError when `req.body` is read
The body is automatically converted to match `CreateFundBody`
questions.explanation: Types are erased, so the annotation is only a claim made to the compiler. Neither Express nor TypeScript validates it. Treat body, query, params and headers as untrusted and validate at the boundary, for example with a Zod schema.

questions.question: What is `DictKey`?
questions.code:
type Dict = { [key: string]: number };
type DictKey = keyof Dict;
questions.explanation: For a string index signature, `keyof` gives `string | number`, because JavaScript converts numeric property keys to strings: `dict[5]` is the same as `dict["5"]`, so number keys are accepted too. A number index signature alone gives just `number`.

questions.question: Why does `Object.keys(investor)` return `string[]` rather than `(keyof Investor)[]`?
options: Because `Object.keys` is written in JavaScript and has no types
Because numeric keys must be converted to strings first
Because typing is structural: a value of type `Investor` may carry extra properties at runtime, so claiming exactly its known keys would be unsafe
questions.explanation: Any object with at least `Investor`'s properties is assignable to `Investor`, so at runtime it may have more keys. Typing the result as `(keyof Investor)[]` would be a lie. Numeric-key conversion is real, but it is not the reason; cast deliberately when you know the object is exact.

questions.question: What is `Arrs`?
questions.code:
type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type Arrs = ToArray<string | number>;
questions.explanation: `T` is a naked type parameter, so the conditional distributes over the union: `ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>`, which is `string[] | number[]`. Wrapping both sides in a tuple (`[T] extends [unknown]`) switches distribution off and gives `(string | number)[]`.

questions.question: What is `N`?
questions.code:
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";
type N = IsString<never>;
questions.explanation: `never` is the empty union. A distributive conditional over a naked type parameter has no members to iterate, so the result is `never` whatever the branches say. To test for `never`, wrap both sides: `[T] extends [never] ? true : false`.

questions.question: What is `P`?
questions.explanation: When `infer` (and therefore `ReturnType`) is applied to an overloaded function, only the last overload signature is used. Here that is `(x: number): number`, so `P` is `number`. It does not union the overloads.

questions.question: How do `Picked` and `Literal` differ?
options: `Picked` keeps `readonly code` and optional `navInr?`; `Literal` loses both modifiers
`Picked` is an error because `K` is not `keyof T`
questions.explanation: A mapped type over `K extends keyof T` is homomorphic and copies the original `readonly` and `?` modifiers, giving `{ readonly code: string; navInr?: number }`. Mapping over a plain union of literals does not, giving `{ code: string; navInr: number | undefined }`. That is why the built-in `Pick` uses `K extends keyof T`.

questions.question: Fill in the blank so that `Mutable<T>` removes the `readonly` modifier from every property: `type Mutable<T> = { ___ [K in keyof T]: T[K] };`
questions.answerHint: Type what goes in the blank
questions.explanation: A `-` prefix removes a modifier in a mapped type: `-readonly` strips readonly and `-?` strips optionality. A plain `readonly` (or `+readonly`) adds it. There is no built-in `Mutable`, which makes this a common interview exercise.

questions.question: What is `HandlerName`?
questions.code:
type DomEvent = "click" | "focus";
type HandlerName = `on${Capitalize<DomEvent>}`;
questions.explanation: `Capitalize` distributes over the union, giving `"Click" | "Focus"`, and the template literal type then prefixes each member with `on`. With several union placeholders, the result is the cross product of all combinations.

questions.question: What is `C`?
questions.explanation: When two `infer` placeholders sit around a delimiter, the first is matched as short as possible, so `Head` is `"funds"` and `Tail` takes the rest, `"equity.large"`. The type is not recursive, so it splits only once rather than into three parts.

questions.question: What happens on the last line?
options: It compiles but throws at runtime
Compile error: a settled payment is not assignable to `Draft`
Compile error: `Extract` cannot be used on a union
questions.explanation: `Extract<Payment, { status: "draft" }>` names just the draft member, so `submit` only accepts drafts. A settled payment's `status` is `"settled"`, which is not `"draft"`, so the call fails to compile. That is how unions restrict which operations apply in which state.

questions.question: How does Zod's `safeParse` differ from `parse`?
options: `safeParse` is faster because it skips nested objects
`safeParse` never throws; it returns a discriminated union you narrow on `success` to reach `data` or `error`
`safeParse` returns the input unchanged when it is invalid
`safeParse` only checks types at compile time
questions.explanation: `parse` returns typed data or throws a `ZodError`. `safeParse` returns `{ success: true, data }` or `{ success: false, error }`, which you narrow on `success`, making it suited to user input where failure is expected. It still validates the whole value at runtime.

questions.question: What are `In` and `Out`?
questions.explanation: `z.input` is the type the schema accepts and `z.output` (the same as `z.infer`) is the type it produces. The schema starts as `z.string()` and the transform turns the string into integer paise, so the input is `string` and the output is `number`. This is "parse, don't validate".

questions.question: A NestJS-style decorator on a constructor parameter (`constructor(@Inject(TOKEN) svc: Svc)`) fails in a project using standard decorators. Why?
options: Standard decorators must be written in lowercase
Standard decorators only run at runtime in Node 24
Parameter decorators (and `emitDecoratorMetadata`) exist only in the legacy `experimentalDecorators` system
questions.explanation: Standard (TC39) decorators use a `(value, context)` signature and support methods, fields, accessors, getters, setters and classes, but not parameters. Parameter decorators and `emitDecoratorMetadata` belong to the legacy `experimentalDecorators` system, which Angular and NestJS rely on.

questions.question: With standard decorators, what does the last line print?
questions.explanation: A field decorator receives `undefined` as its value and may return a function that transforms the initial value. Here the initializer `80` is passed through `Math.min(50, Math.max(0, 80))`, so the field starts as `50`.

questions.question: What is `Seven`?
questions.explanation: `BuildTuple<N>` grows an accumulator tuple until its `length` equals `N`. Spreading a 3-element and a 4-element tuple together gives a 7-element tuple, and its `length` is the numeric literal type `7`. Tuple length is how the type system counts.

questions.question: Under `strict`, which assignment is a compile error?
questions.explanation: `strictFunctionTypes` checks function-typed properties contravariantly, so a handler that only accepts `Dog` cannot be used where any `Animal` may be passed: `pr` errors. Method-shorthand parameters stay bivariant, so `m` compiles, a known soundness hole. Prefer property syntax when you want the strict check.

questions.question: In a repo using project references, which setting must every referenced project have?
questions.explanation: `composite: true` is required on any referenced project. It forces `declaration` on, requires every source file to be matched by `include`/`files`, and enables incremental `.tsbuildinfo` output so `tsc -b` can skip up-to-date projects. `noEmit` would defeat the purpose, since downstream projects consume the emitted `.d.ts` files.

questions.question: Inside an `exports` condition object in `package.json`, why must `"types"` come before `"default"`?
options: npm sorts keys alphabetically when publishing
Conditions are matched in order, so a `types` entry after `default` is never reached
JSON objects require keys in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: Resolvers walk the condition keys in order and stop at the first match. `default` always matches, so a `types` entry placed after it is never used and consumers may see no types. Key order in JSON is significant here; nothing is sorted alphabetically.

questions.question: For a published library, which change to its public types should be treated as a breaking (major) change?
options: Adding an optional property to an input type
Adding a JSDoc comment to a function
Widening a function's return type (e.g. from `string` to `string | null`)
questions.explanation: Consumers rely on the old, narrower return type; code that used the result as a `string` stops compiling once it may be `null`. Narrowing a parameter type, removing exports, adding a required input property and raising the minimum TypeScript version are also breaking. Adding an optional property or a new export is usually minor.

questions.question: In the typed API client, why is `api("listExpenses", {})` a compile error?
options: Zod rejects the empty object at compile time
`BodyArgs` resolves to the empty tuple `[]` for an endpoint without a `body`, so the rest parameter accepts no extra argument (TS2554)
`as const satisfies` makes every endpoint read-only, so it cannot be called
questions.explanation: `listExpenses` has no `body`, so the conditional type `BodyArgs` takes its false branch and produces `[]`. Typing the rest parameter `...args` as `[]` means the call takes exactly one argument, and passing two gives TS2554 "Expected 1 arguments, but got 2". For `createExpense` it produces `[body: ...]`, so omitting the body fails the same way.
